members.prompt:
You have watched a three-round debate on:

> Splitting AI work into clear roles makes it safer and easier to audit and improve than one prompt doing it all

Decide which side argued better — judge argument quality and logical
clarity, not your own opinion of the topic. Announce the winner and
explain your decision in one paragraph.

content: When one prompt does everything (gathering facts, reasoning, drafting, and checking its own work), a failure shows up only as a bad final answer, and you can't tell which step went wrong. Splitting the work into clear roles, such as a retriever, a drafter, and an independent reviewer, turns that black box into a pipeline with inspectable seams. Each handoff produces an artifact you can log, test, and score on its own. If the output is wrong, you can see whether the retriever pulled the wrong document or the drafter misread the right one. That matters for safety, because a separate reviewer with a narrow mandate and no stake in the draft catches errors a model tends to rationalize when grading itself. It also matters for improvement, because you can fix or swap one weak component without retuning a sprawling prompt where every edit risks breaking something unrelated. This is the same reason we separate duties in accounting and code review: no single actor should both produce and approve the work. Role separation doesn't guarantee correctness, but it makes errors visible, attributable, and fixable, and that is what "auditable" means.

**Against:** My opponent's case rests on an analogy that doesn't hold. Separation of duties works in accounting because the clerk and the auditor are different people with different knowledge and incentives. A "retriever," "drafter," and "independent reviewer" are usually the same underlying model in different costumes, so they share the same blind spots. Their errors are correlated, not independent, and a reviewer that misreads a document the way the drafter did will approve the mistake. The "inspectable seams" are also where much of the damage happens. Each handoff compresses context, so the drafter never sees what the retriever discarded, and the reviewer never sees why the drafter chose its framing. Errors then emerge from the interaction itself, which is exactly what attribution struggles with. Studies of multi-agent failures repeatedly find many breakdowns in inter-agent misunderstanding and poorly specified handoffs rather than in any single role.

My strongest point is that splitting the work multiplies failure modes rather than isolating them. Every new role adds another prompt to maintain, another interface to break, and another path for prompt injection to travel from a retrieved document into downstream steps. It also creates a dangerous sense of assurance: a pipeline with a "reviewer" stage looks audited even when the review is a rubber stamp. A single well-structured prompt can still produce inspectable intermediate output: cited sources, explicit reasoning, a separate checklist section. It does this without the context loss and coordination overhead. Role separation can help in specific cases, especially when a stage is truly different, such as a deterministic validator or a human. But as a general rule, adding more parts gives you more logs, not more safety.

My opponent concedes the key point: stages help when they are truly different, such as a deterministic validator, a different model, or a human. But you can only insert those checks at a seam, so role separation is what makes diverse, uncorrelated review possible in the first place. The correlated-error worry also cuts the other way. Research on LLM self-correction (e.g., Huang et al., 2023) finds that models often fail to fix their own reasoning without external feedback. A reviewer that never sees the drafter's framing is less anchored to it, not more. Context loss at handoffs is real, but it is visible: you can log exactly what the retriever discarded and test it. In a single prompt, that same "discarding" happens silently inside attention. And the claim that one prompt can show its work through cited sources and explicit reasoning overlooks that self-reported reasoning is often unfaithful (Turpin et al., 2023). A retriever's output is a record of what was actually fetched, not the model's story about it. My new argument turns their injection point around: separation enables least privilege. In patterns like the "dual-LLM" design or CaMeL, the component that reads untrusted documents has no tools and no authority. The component that can act never sees raw untrusted text. A single do-everything prompt must hold both the poisoned input and the power to act in the same context, which is exactly the setup prompt injection exploits. More parts do mean more interfaces to maintain, but they are the only way to keep untrusted input and authority apart.

**Against:** My opponent's best examples prove my point. CaMeL and the dual-LLM pattern are not safe because work is split into roles. They are safe because a deterministic layer enforces capability limits and tracks which data is tainted. The quarantined model's output is treated as untrusted data and never read as instructions. Ordinary role splits lack that enforcement. A "researcher" agent summarizes a poisoned page and hands the summary to an "executor" agent with tools. That launders the injection: the attacker's text now arrives as trusted internal output. So the security comes from the enforcement mechanism, not the division of labor, and splitting without it can make things worse. The faithfulness argument also cuts both ways. A drafter's handoff note is just as much a self-report as a single prompt's reasoning. Meanwhile, a single agent's tool calls and retrieved documents are logged just as precisely as a separate retriever's. On Huang et al., the same paper found that multi-agent debate did no better than simple self-consistency once the number of responses was held equal. Extra LLM "reviewers" were not the external feedback that helped.

My strongest remaining argument is that the promised modular improvement is largely an illusion. Each stage gets its own metric, so teams optimize the retriever for recall and the drafter for fluency, and those local gains often fail to improve end-to-end quality. A retriever "improved" to return more documents can bury the one fact the drafter needed. You still have to evaluate the whole pipeline, and per-stage scores invite blame-shifting and Goodhart effects rather than real attribution. Fixed decompositions also lock in today's guess about how a task should be split. As models improve, they can often do the combined task better than the pipeline, but the scaffolding stays in place because every stage has its own tests and owners. Use real separation where it adds something different in kind: deterministic validators, capability boundaries, or human approval. As a general rule, though, carving one model's work into roles mostly adds overhead that looks like an audit trail.

**For:** My opponent's Goodhart worry argues for end-to-end evaluation, which I never opposed. It does not argue against stage artifacts. An end-to-end score tells you *that* the system failed, and stage outputs tell you *where*. Their own example shows this: if a retriever buries a key fact, you can only find that out by looking at the retriever's output and seeing that the fact was there and the drafter missed it. Without that artifact, the same failure is just "worse answers." Lock-in also cuts the other way. When evals show a newer model does the combined task better, a modular pipeline lets you merge two stages and measure the difference. A sprawling monolithic prompt is just as frozen, but nobody can say which instructions are still doing any work. On CaMeL, I agree that deterministic enforcement provides the security. But enforcement needs a boundary to act on. Taint tracking and capability limits only work if the system is already split into components with separate inputs and powers. Their "laundering" example describes a bad split, not an argument against splitting. My new point is that clear roles make risk-proportionate oversight possible. With defined stages, you can send only the risky step, such as an outbound payment or a published claim, to a human or a strict validator, and let low-stakes steps run freely. A single prompt forces a cruder choice: review everything, which humans won't sustain, or review nothing. Separation lets scarce human attention go where the stakes are. That is not overhead that looks like an audit trail. It is how audits actually get done.

**Against:** My opponent's risk-proportionate oversight doesn't require splitting the model's thinking into roles. It requires gating *actions*, and a single agent already exposes those as discrete tool calls. Most agent frameworks put the human approval on the tool call itself: "send_payment" or "publish" pauses for sign-off while reading and drafting run freely. The boundary sits at the tool layer, not between a "drafter" persona and a "reviewer" persona. The same applies to taint tracking and to their buried-fact example. A single agent's retrieval calls are logged verbatim, so you can see that the fact was fetched and then ignored without adding a separate retriever. Each time my opponent identifies something that actually helps, whether enforcement, diverse checkers, human gates, or logged artifacts, it turns out to live at tool and action boundaries that a single agent already has. Their own phrase, "a bad split," gives the game away. The topic claims that splitting makes systems safer, but splitting helps only when it coincides with these hard boundaries, and then the boundaries are doing the work.

My strongest remaining argument is cost. Multi-agent designs routinely use several times more tokens and latency. Anthropic, for example, reported that its multi-agent research system used roughly 15x the tokens of a chat interaction. Practitioner guides, including Anthropic's own "Building effective agents," advise starting with the simplest single-agent design and adding agents only when they demonstrably help. That budget has alternatives: a stronger model, more end-to-end evals, sampling multiple answers, or more human review at the action gates where it matters. So the honest rule is to put hard checks where stakes are high and keep the cognition unified. Carving one model into roles is sometimes worth it, but as a default it spends real money on the appearance of independence rather than on the checks that actually make systems safe and auditable.
Against wins. They showed, step by step, that each benefit For cited actually comes from hard boundaries a single agent already has, not from splitting the work into roles.

output.reasoning: Both sides argued well and cited evidence, but Against had the sharper logic and steadily narrowed what the motion could claim. For opened with a clear case: inspectable seams, an independent reviewer, the separation-of-duties analogy, and easier modular fixes. Against weakened that case early with the point about correlated errors, since the 'roles' are often the same model sharing the same blind spots, and noted that context loss at handoffs creates new failure modes. For's second round was its strongest, especially the least-privilege argument from the dual-LLM and CaMeL designs. Against then turned those same examples around: their security comes from deterministic enforcement and taint tracking, not from dividing the work, and naive splits can 'launder' an injection by passing attacker text along as trusted internal output. For's later replies (stage artifacts locate failures, enforcement needs a boundary, risk-proportionate oversight) were reasonable. But Against answered each one by showing it relies on tool and action boundaries a single agent already exposes: logged retrieval calls, approval gates on actions like payments, and capability limits. Against also seized on For's phrase 'a bad split,' arguing that splitting helps only when it coincides with those hard boundaries, which then do the real work. This undercut the motion's general claim that role separation itself makes systems safer and more auditable. Against's cost argument was somewhat loose: the 15x token figure compares a multi-agent system with ordinary chat, not with a single agent doing the same task. It was also a final-round point For could not answer, so it counted for little. Even so, Against's core distinction between role decomposition and enforcement boundaries went largely unrefuted. For never fully explained why splitting cognition into personas, as opposed to gating actions, adds safety beyond what those boundaries already provide.
